passage:
Every lunch break, Mrs Kurian stood on duty near the art room steps, where she could see the whole playground. In June, Thomas and Chinmay still sat together with one sketchbook between them, drawing robots.
By August, Thomas had been picked for the under-eleven football team. Now at the bell he sprinted straight to the field, boots knocking against his bag. Chinmay went up the art room steps, where a group was painting a mural of the school garden.
Some days Thomas glanced at the steps before running off. Once Chinmay waved a paintbrush when Thomas scored a goal.
Mrs Kurian thought about calling them in for a talk, then didn't. There was no fight to fix. In the staffroom she told a colleague, "They haven't fallen out. They've just grown in different directions this term."

qa.q: Which team was Thomas picked for?
qa.a: Thomas was picked for the under-eleven football team.

qa.q: What might Thomas's glance at the steps suggest he is thinking?
qa.a: It suggests Thomas still thinks about Chinmay and may feel a small pull between the old friend and the new team.

qa.q: Why was Mrs Kurian wise not to call them in for a talk?
qa.a: No one had done anything wrong, so a talk might have made them feel they had failed; watching quietly lets the change happen naturally.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel about Thomas running to the field every day?
qa.a: Chinmay may miss the robot drawings a little but also enjoys the mural group, and the paintbrush wave shows there is still warmth.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing two friends drifting into football and art groups with no one at fault.

passage:
I've taught Karthik and Sabina since Class 3, and last year you couldn't separate them. They shared a tiffin, a pencil sharpener, even a cold, I think.
This term I've watched something shift. Karthik stays after school for football practice now; I see him in the corridor with mud up to his knees, talking goals with four other boys. Sabina has joined the art club and spends lunch in the art room with Esther and Pooja, making clay birds for the annual day.
I don't think anything happened between them. I haven't seen a quarrel, no sulking at each other's desks. When Karthik scored in the inter-house match, Sabina clapped from the art room window. I can't say what either of them feels. Maybe they miss each other, maybe not yet. It looks to me as if their days simply went different ways.

qa.q: What is Sabina making in the art room?
qa.a: Sabina is making clay birds for the annual day with Esther and Pooja.

qa.q: Why does the teacher say 'I can't say what either of them feels'?
qa.a: The teacher feels uncertain, seeing only what the children do, not what's inside; there seems to be no quarrel, but the teacher can't tell whether Karthik and Sabina miss each other.

qa.q: How could the teacher support both children through this change?
qa.a: The teacher could leave the new groups alone while offering small chances to mix, like a class project, so the old friendship stays kind without being forced.

qa.q: What would change if the teacher had seen a quarrel?
qa.a: Then there might be hurt to help them repair; without one, it is just new activities pulling them apart, and no one needs to be blamed.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher observing two former close friends moving into football and art circles without any wrongdoing.
